1205.title: karma: the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita
1205.hook: an old beggar's bowl is snatched from his hands, and he answers with a song that won't even blame karma
1205.howItsDone: The song of the brahmin of Avanti, sometimes called the Bhikshu Gita, is read by students of the Bhagavata's eleventh book as a teaching on bearing insult and on the mind as the source of joy and sorrow.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma as the road for people who still want things, walked until weariness or faith arrives.
screen: `ACTION FOR THOSE WHO STILL WANT.` · `NOW, THE BEGGAR'S SONG.`

segments.voice: A begging bowl, snatched out of an old man's hands. His staff, taken. His water pot, gone. Someone throws dirt at him; someone spits. Krishna tells this story when Uddhava admits how hard it is to bear the insults of others. The old man was once rich, a brahmin from Avanti, and a miser who never enjoyed his money or gave any of it away. Then, piece by piece, it was gone. Something turned in him. He left home as a wandering beggar, and the people of the town made sport of him. What he says back is a song, and it refuses to blame anyone you'd expect.
screen: `A BOWL SNATCHED AWAY.` → `A MISER WHO LOST EVERYTHING.` → `HE ANSWERS WITH A SONG.`

segments.voice: The song is sometimes called the Bhikshu Gita, the beggar's song. Its center, in paraphrase: these people aren't the cause of my joy and sorrow. Nor are the gods, nor my body, nor the planets, nor my karma, nor time. The mind is the cause. The mind turns the wheel. Look who's on that list. Karma. In a week about action, a man in the Uddhava Gita declines to blame even his own past deeds for what he feels now. He isn't saying karma isn't real. He's saying the place where sorrow gets made is closer than that. Then he takes the list apart, one suspect at a time. If other people are the cause, it's one body knocking against another; what does the self have to do with it? When your own teeth bite your own tongue, who is there to be angry at? If the gods are the cause, what does that have to do with a self that doesn't change? And on down the list. When something stings, the first move is to find who's to blame: them, the traffic, bad luck, even karma. The beggar keeps walking down the list to the one item he can actually work with, his own mind. That's Krishna's answer to Uddhava about bearing hard words. Not pretending they didn't hurt. Looking at where the hurt is being made.
screen: `NOT THEM, NOT THE GODS, NOT KARMA.` · `THE MIND TURNS THE WHEEL.` · `TEETH THAT BITE YOUR OWN TONGUE.` · `START WITH WHAT YOU CAN WORK WITH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small sorrow from this week and walk the beggar's list slowly: was it them, the day, your body, your luck? Give each suspect its moment, then come to the last stop, your own mind, and simply watch what it's doing with that sorrow, without fixing it. If you pray, you can bring that mind, just as it is, to the One you pray to.
Karma. In the beggar's song even karma isn't blamed: the mind is named as the place where joy and sorrow turn.
screen: `KARMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: karma, the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita. The wheel turns in the mind, and that's where the work can start. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1205 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KARMA: THE BHAGAVATA'S UDDHAVA GITA.`

1206.title: karma: the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita
1206.hook: Krishna sorts workers the way a foreman might, by what drives them, and then adds a worker the strands can't hold
1206.howItsDone: Hindu teachers use the three gunas to talk about the quality of everyday work and food and habits, and in the Bhagavata's eleventh book Krishna applies them to the worker and the work, with a fourth kind beyond the gunas for one who takes refuge in him.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beggar's song: not them, not the gods, not even karma. The mind turns the wheel.
screen: `THE MIND TURNS THE WHEEL.` · `NOW, THE WORKER.`

segments.voice: What kind of worker are you? Not how fast, not how skilled. What's going on inside while the work gets done. Near the end of the dialogue, Krishna sorts workers the way a careful foreman might, by what drives them. He reaches for the three strands from the Samkhya weeks, sattva, rajas and tamas: clear, restless, heavy. Every kind of work can be read through them, he says, and so can every worker. Then, at the end of the list, he names one more worker, a kind the strands can't hold.
screen: `WHAT KIND OF WORKER ARE YOU?` → `THE THREE STRANDS RETURN.` → `ONE MORE WORKER.`

segments.voice: Here's the sorting, in paraphrase. A worker free of attachment is in sattva. A worker blinded by wanting things for himself is in rajas. A worker who has lost the sense of what to do and what not to do is in tamas. And a worker who has taken refuge in him, Krishna says, is beyond the strands altogether. He reads the work the same way. Work offered to him, done without hunger for its fruit, is sattvic. Work done for what it will bring is rajasic. Work done to harm is tamasic. Notice what isn't on the list: any particular job. The strands don't sort cleaners from surgeons. They sort the inside. Two people can carry the same boxes up the same stairs for a friend who's moving, one for praise and one as an offering, and in these verses they're doing different work. On the path of action, the task is the same size for everyone. What changes is the hand behind it. And the fourth worker? Krishna doesn't describe a better technique. He describes a relationship: refuge. For devotees of Krishna, that's where the path of action is headed. For anyone else listening, the first three are already a mirror.
screen: `FREE, DRIVEN, OR FOGGED.` · `WORK OFFERED, WORK FOR GAIN, WORK TO HARM.` · `THE STRANDS SORT THE WORKER, NOT THE JOB.` · `A FOURTH WORKER: BEYOND THE STRANDS.`

segments.voice: Picture starting the next task waiting for you, a phone call, an email, a drive, and notice what's already there inside: an eagerness for a result, a heaviness, a calm, with no grading. Then picture starting it once more, and see whether simply noticing what drives you changes anything. If you pray, you can offer that task to the One you pray to.
Karma. Work, sorted in the Uddhava Gita by the worker's inside: unattached, driven, fogged, or beyond the strands altogether.
screen: `KARMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: karma, the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita. Same boxes, same stairs; the difference is the hand. Rest well.

screen: `DAY 1206 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KARMA: THE BHAGAVATA'S UDDHAVA GITA.`

1207.title: karma: the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita
1207.hook: after the whole long teaching, Uddhava says it's too hard, and Krishna's answer is short and gentle
1207.howItsDone: Vaishnava Hindus speak of offering their daily work to Krishna, and the eleventh book of the Bhagavata, where Krishna tells Uddhava to do all his work for his sake and to see him in every being, is one of the texts they draw on.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma sorted the worker: free, driven, fogged, or beyond the strands.
screen: `FREE, DRIVEN, OR FOGGED.` · `THE CLOSE OF THE DIALOGUE.`

segments.voice: After all of it, the earth, the three paths, the beggar's song, the strands, Uddhava says something brave. He tells Krishna that the yoga he's described is hard for anyone who can't master the mind. Hard, he says in effect, for people like us. Give us something a person can actually do. It's a student raising a hand at the end of a long lecture: I didn't get all that. Krishna doesn't sigh or start over. His answer is short, and surprisingly gentle.
screen: `THIS IS TOO HARD.` → `GIVE US SOMETHING DOABLE.` → `A SHORT, GENTLE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Krishna's answer, in paraphrase: do all your work for my sake, remembering me, slowly, little by little. That's it. No new technique. The work stays the same: the cooking, the trading, the caring for children and parents. What changes is who it's for. Then he widens it. See me in every being, he says, inside them and outside them, the way the sky is in everything. And then a line that asks a great deal: bow down to everyone, even to a dog, a donkey, a cow, even to the person your society pushes to the edges, and don't mind if your own people laugh at you. The text names the creatures and people its own world looked past, and asks the devotee to bow there too. Notice that word, slowly. Not a crash course. A lifetime of small handings-over, one task at a time. Then the dialogue ends. Krishna sends Uddhava to Badari, a hermitage in the mountains, to live what he has heard. And Uddhava, who began by begging to go along, goes where he's sent instead. The Uddhava Gita closes with a student walking away from his teacher, carrying the work. Tomorrow, the word for that kind of carrying.
screen: `DO ALL YOUR WORK FOR ME, SLOWLY.` · `SEE ME IN EVERY BEING.` · `BOW EVEN WHERE OTHERS PASS BY.` · `UDDHAVA GOES WHERE HE'S SENT.`

segments.voice: Choose one small piece of work waiting for you and picture doing it start to finish at an unhurried pace, giving it away before you even begin. If you pray, you can offer it to the One you pray to; if you don't, offer it to the person it will serve, and let the breath stay slow.
Karma. At the close of the Uddhava Gita: all your work, done for the one you love, slowly, little by little.
screen: `KARMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: karma, the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita. Slowly, little by little, is how the text says it's done. I'll be here tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1207 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SEVA AS VOCATION.`

1208.title: seva as vocation
1208.hook: a week of goodbyes ends with a student carrying the work away, and the track names what he carries: seva
1208.howItsDone: In Hindu temples and homes, seva names the care given to the deity and to others, such as cooking, cleaning and preparing flowers, and some Hindus describe their daily work itself as seva offered to God.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the Uddhava Gita and its week of karma, one long goodbye: Uddhava asked to go along and got a teaching; the earth didn't swerve; a mocked beggar named his own mind; workers were sorted by what drives them; and at the end, do all your work for me, slowly.
screen: `ALL YOUR WORK, SLOWLY.` · `THE WEEK, LOOKING BACK.`

segments.voice: Someone is cooking for the temple. Someone is sweeping. Someone is stringing flowers for the deity. None of it looks like scripture. Back on day fifteen, Hanuman carried a mountain, and the word was seva. Now it comes back with a second half. What do you call a whole life built out of Krishna's last line to Uddhava, do all your work for me? The track's next word has an answer: seva as vocation.
screen: `COOKING, SWEEPING, STRINGING FLOWERS.` → `SEVA COMES BACK.` → `WHAT DO YOU CALL THAT LIFE?`

segments.voice: Seva means service: attending on someone, honoring them by caring for them. In Hindu temples, it's the word for the care given to the deity and to the people who come, from cooking to sweeping to stringing flowers. And the word reaches back into the texts. In the Bhagavata's seventh book, the boy Prahlada lists the ways a person can love Vishnu: hearing about him, singing of him, remembering him, then serving his feet, worship, bowing, being his servant, being his friend, and offering oneself completely. Serving and servanthood sit right in the middle. Seva isn't a side project of devotion. It's one of its main rooms. Now, vocation. Near the end of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that a person who worships the source of all beings through their own work, the work that is theirs to do, reaches perfection. Next to the Uddhava Gita's last lesson, the two fit. Uddhava was told to do all his work for Krishna. The Gita says the work itself, done as worship, is the offering. That's seva as vocation: not a few good deeds squeezed in around a job, but the job, the household, the caring, all of it done as service. The next few days look at it in a tree, a hungry king, and an honored guest who washed feet at a great feast.
screen: `SEVA: SERVICE, ATTENDING ON.` · `PRAHLADA: SERVING, SERVANTHOOD.` · `WORSHIP HIM WITH YOUR OWN WORK.` · `NOT BESIDE THE JOB: THE JOB ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Go back over the last few days and find one place your work, paid or unpaid, actually served someone: a meal made, a report someone needed, a ride given. Don't inflate it; hold that person in mind, and let the work become, for a moment, something you gave. If you pray, you can offer that work to the One you pray to.
Seva as vocation. Seva is service, attending on God and on others. As a vocation, it's a life's work done as that kind of service.
screen: `SEVA AS VOCATION — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: seva as vocation. The job itself can be the offering. See you tomorrow.

1209.title: seva as vocation
1209.hook: midday heat, cowherd boys resting in the shade, and Krishna starts praising the trees
1209.howItsDone: Hindu teachers point to Krishna's praise of the trees in the Bhagavata's tenth book as a picture of service, and its closing verse, on doing good with life, wealth, understanding and words, is recited in talks on seva.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: seva as vocation. Not good deeds squeezed in around the job, but the job itself done as service.
screen: `THE JOB ITSELF AS SERVICE.` · `A TEACHER IN THE SHADE.`

segments.voice: Midday, far out in the forest, and the sun is fierce. Krishna and the cowherd boys have taken the cows a long way from the village, and the boys are hot and worn out. They duck under the trees for shade. A rest stop, nothing more. And Krishna looks up into the branches and starts talking about the trees, the way you'd talk about a person you admire. It's a short scene in the Bhagavata's tenth book, in the middle of a summer day, and it holds a whole picture of service.
screen: `MIDDAY, FAR FROM THE VILLAGE.` → `BOYS IN THE SHADE.` → `KRISHNA PRAISES THE TREES.`

segments.voice: Look at these blessed trees, he says, in paraphrase. They live entirely for others. They bear wind and rain, heat and frost themselves, and they shelter us from all of it. Then he lists what a tree gives: its leaves, flowers and fruit, its shade, its roots, bark and wood, its fragrance and sap, even its ashes, even its young shoots. No one who comes to a tree goes away with nothing. Then the verse that turns the scene into a teaching. This much, he says, is the fruit of being born: to keep doing good for others with your life, your wealth, your understanding and your words. Notice the four. That's a list built for a vocation, because everyone has at least one. Some days the seva is money. Some days it's what you know. Some days it's your hours and your hands. And some days it's only a word, but a word is on the list. The tree doesn't pick one gift and refuse the rest. It gives whatever part of it is asked for. And notice who's listening. Not sages. Boys who look after cows. Krishna doesn't take them to a temple to learn about service. He points at the shade they're already sitting in.
screen: `THEY LIVE ENTIRELY FOR OTHERS.` · `LEAF, FRUIT, SHADE, BARK, EVEN ASH.` · `LIFE, WEALTH, UNDERSTANDING, WORDS.` · `A LESSON IN THE SHADE YOU SIT IN.`

segments.voice: Let Krishna's four gifts come one at a time: life, where your time could help someone; wealth, something small to give; understanding, something you know that someone needs; words, who could use a kind one. Don't plan it all; let one of the four light up and rest there, offering it to the One you pray to, if you pray.
Seva as vocation. Service as a life's work: like the tree, giving with life, wealth, understanding and words.
screen: `SEVA AS VOCATION — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: seva as vocation. Even a kind word counts as giving. Go gently.

1210.title: seva as vocation
1210.hook: after a long fast, a king finally sits down to a meal, and the guests start arriving
1210.howItsDone: Rantideva's story from the Bhagavata's ninth book is told by Hindu teachers as a picture of selfless service, and his wish to bear the pain of all beings is quoted in talks on compassion and seva.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva as vocation came from the trees: life, wealth, understanding and words, given to whoever asks.
screen: `LIFE, WEALTH, UNDERSTANDING, WORDS.` · `A KING AT HIS TABLE.`

segments.voice: A king who has already given away everything he owns sits down to eat. He and his family have gone a long stretch without food, without even water. Now, at last, a meal: a little ghee, some milk, a porridge, a cup of water. Hands reach for the bowls. And then someone comes to the door. The king is Rantideva, and the Bhagavata's ninth book tells his story in a handful of verses. It's a short story. It doesn't feel short when you're the one holding the bowl.
screen: `A LONG FAST, THEN A MEAL.` → `SOMEONE AT THE DOOR.` → `RANTIDEVA.`

segments.voice: The first to come is a brahmin guest. Rantideva sees God in his guest and feeds him gladly. He divides what's left with his family, and another guest arrives, a laborer, and he feeds him too. Then comes a man with a pack of hungry dogs, and Rantideva gives him the rest of the food, honoring the man and the dogs alike. Now only water is left. One more person comes, a man his society shut out as an outcaste, dying of thirst, asking for water. Rantideva, nearly dying of thirst himself, gives it. Then he says the words the story is remembered for. In paraphrase: I don't ask God for the highest state, with all its powers, nor even for freedom from rebirth. I ask to stand inside all beings and bear their pain, so that they can be free of it. Then a turn. The guests, the story says, were the lords of the worlds themselves, come in disguise. They reveal themselves, ready to grant anything. Rantideva bows, and asks for nothing. Two things for a vocation of seva. Every guest gets the same honor: the line runs from the honored to the shunned, and his care doesn't shrink as he goes down it. And he doesn't serve to get somewhere. Not heaven, not even freedom. The service is the destination.
screen: `GUEST AFTER GUEST, THE SAME HONOR.` · `ONLY WATER LEFT, AND HE GIVES IT.` · `NOT HEAVEN, NOT FREEDOM: THEIR PAIN.` · `THE GUESTS WERE THE GODS.`

segments.voice: Picture a small meal on a table, yours, and let people you know come to the door one at a time: someone easy to give to, someone harder, someone you'd usually walk past. You don't have to hand anything over; just notice the moment of reluctance with each one, and breathe through it. If you pray, you can hold each guest before the One you pray to.
Seva as vocation. Service as a whole life: Rantideva gives each guest the same honor, down to the last cup of water, and asks nothing back.
screen: `SEVA AS VOCATION — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: seva as vocation. Honor doesn't run out before the last guest. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1210 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SEVA AS VOCATION.`

1211.title: seva as vocation
1211.hook: jobs are handed out for a king's great sacrifice, and the guest of honor takes the one at the guests' feet
1211.howItsDone: At Hindu temple festivals and family ceremonies, volunteers take on the cooking, serving, cleaning and welcoming as seva, and stories like Krishna washing guests' feet at the Rajasuya are told to honor that work.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva as vocation was Rantideva at his table: the same honor for every guest, down to the last cup of water.
screen: `THE SAME HONOR FOR EVERY GUEST.` · `JOBS AT A GREAT FEAST.`

segments.voice: A great royal sacrifice is underway, and someone has to hand out the jobs. King Yudhishthira is holding the Rajasuya, the rite that marks a king as sovereign, and kings and sages have come from everywhere. There are crowds to feed, gifts to give, money to guard, elders to look after. So everyone pitches in, the way families do before a big wedding. And Krishna, the guest this same story has the assembly honor first, has a job too. The Bhagavata's tenth book tells you which one, almost in passing.
screen: `A KING'S GREAT SACRIFICE.` → `EVERYONE GETS A JOB.` → `WHICH JOB DOES KRISHNA TAKE?`

segments.voice: Here's the Bhagavata's list. Bhima ran the kitchen. Duryodhana kept the treasury. Sahadeva received the guests, Nakula gathered supplies, and Arjuna looked after the elders. Draupadi served the food. Karna handed out the gifts. And Krishna washed the feet of the guests. In this same story, the assembly gives Krishna the first honor of the whole ceremony. For his devotees, he is God. And his job is at the guests' feet, with water, washing off the dust of the road. In tradition, water for a guest's feet is part of the welcome. It's also work done kneeling. He does it anyway, and the text mentions it in passing, inside a list, as though nothing could be more natural. For a vocation of seva, that short list does two things. It shows that every job at the feast was service: the treasury and the kitchen, the gifts and the plates. Nobody on that list was there just to be seen. And it shows that the job doesn't measure the person. The one honored first worked at the feet. On an ordinary Tuesday, the trash bags, the folding chairs, the sign-in table aren't lesser roles in this picture. In the Bhagavata, that's where Krishna stands.
screen: `KITCHEN, TREASURY, GUESTS, GIFTS.` · `KRISHNA WASHES THE GUESTS' FEET.` · `HONORED FIRST, KNEELING AT THEIR FEET.` · `THE JOB DOESN'T MEASURE THE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Think of a place you'll be this week where things need doing, home, work, a temple, a family gathering, and notice the job you'd hope someone else takes. Picture yourself doing that one gladly, with nobody noticing. If you pray, you can offer that unchosen work to the One you pray to.
Seva as vocation. Service as a life's work: at Yudhishthira's sacrifice every job is service, and the guest of honor washes feet.
screen: `SEVA AS VOCATION — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: seva as vocation. The lowest job at the feast went to the one honored first. That's today, done.

screen: `DAY 1211 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SEVA AS VOCATION.`
